Chapter 6: Overcoming Setbacks—Navigating Obstacles and Relapses.
Even if you've got a clear-headed rider, a motivated elephant, and a path that seems well thought out, setbacks are just part of the deal. Change hardly ever follows a straight, predictable line—it’s more like a winding trail, full of dips and unexpected twists. The real trick isn’t dodging every single obstacle, but learning to expect them and respond with some resilience and flexibility.
Let’s be honest—setbacks can stir up a ton of frustration or self-doubt. That’s when your elephant wants to throw in the towel, and your rider might start overthinking everything. But here’s something to remember: setbacks aren’t some weird exception—they’re a natural part of making any kind of change. Think about a hiker tackling a long trail. They don’t panic when they hit a rough patch—they just keep moving, knowing it’s part of the journey. In the same way, anyone working on change—whether it's personal or with a team—should expect a few slips or slowdowns along the way.
So, what’s a smart way to deal with these bumps in the road? Try reframing obstacles as chances to learn. If a new habit starts to slip, or a team slides back into old routines, pause for a second and ask yourself: What made this tough? Was the path unclear, the goal a bit fuzzy, or maybe motivation was just running low? Taking a moment for this gentle self-check helps you spot what needs tweaking—maybe you need to clarify the next step, line up better support, or shift something in your environment.
If you want to bounce back from setbacks, here are a few gentle strategies that really help:
First, plan for relapses. Assume you’ll hit a bump at some point, and decide ahead of time how you’ll handle it. Next, practice self-compassion. When things don’t go as planned, treat yourself—or your team—with kindness instead of criticism. And finally, analyze, adjust, and give it another shot. Every obstacle is just feedback, not a final verdict.
For example, imagine a team misses a new reporting deadline. Instead of pointing fingers, leaders can step back and ask if the process was clear enough, or if reminders were sent out on time. Or say someone’s trying to eat healthier but slips into old habits for a week. Rather than feeling defeated, they can look at what triggered the lapse and plan for it next time.
When you treat setbacks as just another part of the journey—not as failures—the whole process of change feels a lot more doable and way less stressful. This kind of mindset keeps both your rider and your elephant engaged, even when the trail gets rocky.
